learning_objective: 🎯 Learn how to write for the fast-paced world of journalism, radio, TV, and digital platforms with extreme clarity, accuracy, and impact!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: News writing uses the 'Inverted Pyramid' structure. The most critical information (the 5 Ws: Who, What, When, Where, Why) goes in the very first paragraph (the Lead). Background details go at the bottom.
Hard news is factual, objective, and urgent (e.g., an earthquake report). Feature writing is longer, more descriptive, and focuses on human interest, emotion, or background stories.
Unlike newspapers, broadcast scripts are 'written for the ear'. Sentences must be short, conversational, and easy to read aloud without running out of breath. Numbers are usually rounded off.
Writing for the web requires scannability. Readers skim screens, so writers use bold headings, bullet points, hyperlinks, and SEO (Search Engine Optimization) to grab attention quickly.

fun_activity.title: 🗞️ The 5-W Lead Challenge
fun_activity.instructions: Take a famous fairy tale (like Little Red Riding Hood). Rewrite its opening as a hard-hitting newspaper 'Lead' paragraph using only the 5 Ws (Who, What, When, Where, Why) in exactly one sentence!

exam_tips: 📌 Always remember the 5 Ws and 1 H (Who, What, Where, When, Why, How)—they form the foundation of journalistic writing.
📌 The Inverted Pyramid is essential for editors because it allows them to cut the bottom of an article for space without losing key facts.
📌 When asked about Broadcast vs. Print, emphasize that broadcast is 'conversational and auditory' while print is 'detailed and visual'.
quick_recap: ⭐ Media writing must be concise, accurate, and tailored to the target audience.
⭐ The Inverted Pyramid prioritizes the most important news at the very top.
⭐ Writing for the web requires a different format focusing on scannability and quick engagement.
